# Creating the models and chosing the best

## Setting up the environment

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(tree)
library(baguette)
```

## Importing the data, creating splits and folds.

This modeling code was created to explore data from the CDC's NHANES survey. While the full dataset has more variables, a EPOST colleague, Dr. Laura Callis, sent this dataset around about a week ago. She had selected 7 which are related to heart rates, blood pressures, and caffine intake.

From the CDC's Website (while it lasts): The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) collects data about the health of adults and children in the United States. We also collect data about what participants eat, drink, and take as supplements to determine how many nutrients are in their diet. These dietary interviews and blood tests help us measure the nutritional status of U.S. adults and children. Learn more at the https://wwwn.cdc.gov/nchs/nhanes/.

First I want to pull in this NHANES data of 18 to 29 year-olds:

```{r}
NHANES <- read.csv("data/NHANES_EnergyDrinks_BP_ages18-29.csv", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

Because this data is not administrative, like the datasets we used in class, where every cell had a value, we need to address the missing value issue. Regression models would handle this well by just pairwise removing observations with a missing value, but our random forests cannot handle these kinds of missing values, so I'm just going to preemtively remove them.

```{r}
NHANES <- NHANES |>
  select(-Cycle, -RecallDays) |>
  tidyr::drop_na(Pulse)
save(NHANES, file = "data/NHANES.RData")
```

Now we will split the data into training and testing subsets

```{r}
set.seed(852006)
NHANES_split <- rsample::initial_split(NHANES, prop = .7)
	NHANES_train <- training(NHANES_split)
	NHANES_test <- testing(NHANES_split)
```

I used a 5 fold cross-validation to select the best model each family of models, setting up my own grid of tuning parameters for each model.

```{r}
NHANES_CV_folds <- vfold_cv(NHANES_train, 5)
```

## Creating Models

Honestly, the numeric variables in this dataset are not great as response variables to the other predictors, but I believe the goal here is proof of concept, and not statistical rigor. I have chosen two possible outcome variables: text_messages_sent_yesterday and doing_homework_hours. After tinkering with both of them, I decided to use text_messages_sent_yesterday as my response variable, and the reminaing variables as my predictors.

### Regression Tree Model

Since I am not using a categorical outcome variable, I'm not going to use a classification tree, but a regression tree instead. Regression tress create decision points, often called splits, which determine how to split the data into groups which will minimize the residual's sum of squares within each of the nodes which follow.

```{r}
# Outcome Vars: Systolic_BP
# Predictor Vars: Diastolic_BP, Pulse, Age, Sex, EnergyDrink, Caffeine_mg


tree_rec <- recipe(Systolic_BP ~ Diastolic_BP + Pulse + Age + Sex + EnergyDrink + Caffeine_mg, 
                   data = NHANES_train) |>
  step_naomit(all_predictors()) |>
  # don't normalize the outcome, but do the rest:
  step_normalize(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) |>
  # create dummys:
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())
tree_rec

tree_mod <- decision_tree(tree_depth = tune(),
                          min_n = tune(),
                          cost_complexity = tune()) |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")
  
tree_wkf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  add_model(tree_mod)
```

Here I have decided to use RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error) as my primary metric of performance. Text Messages Sent is a continuous numeric variable, which means RMSE is well suited to interpret results, and to penalize large prediction errors more heavilyt than Mean Absolute Error. Hopefully that will encourage the tuning to select a model that avoids large mispredicitions.

```{r}
tree_grid <- grid_regular(cost_complexity(),
                          tree_depth(),
                          min_n(),
                          levels = c(10, 5, 5))
tree_fits <- tree_wkf |> 
  tune_grid(resamples = NHANES_CV_folds,
            grid = tree_grid)

tree_fits |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  mutate(tree_depth = factor(tree_depth)) |>
  ggplot(aes(cost_complexity, mean, color = tree_depth)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ .metric, scales = "free", nrow = 2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_number()) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "plasma", begin = .9, end = 0)
```

#### Select the best regression tree and finalize the workflow

```{r}
tree_fits |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |>
  arrange(mean)

tree_best_params <- select_best(tree_fits, metric = "rmse")
tree_best_params

tree_final_wkf <- tree_wkf |>
  finalize_workflow(tree_best_params)

tree_final_fit <- tree_final_wkf |>
  last_fit(NHANES_split)
tree_final_fit

tree_final_fit |>
  collect_metrics()

tree_final_model <- extract_workflow(tree_final_fit) 
tree_final_model

tree_final_model |>
  extract_fit_engine() |>
  rpart.plot::rpart.plot(roundint = FALSE)
```

Okay, so this is obviously not ideal, in that the cost complexity selected by the cross-valudation was so large it pruned the tree down to a single node. This may well be because of the nature of this data, so I'm going to continue forward.

### Random Forest Models

```{r}
rf_spec <- rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) |>
  set_engine("ranger", importance = "impurity") |>
  set_mode("regression")

rf_wkf <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(tree_rec) |>
  add_model(rf_spec)
```

#### Tune using the training-set cross-validation folds

```{r}
rf_grid <- grid_regular(
  mtry(range = c(2, 6)),
  min_n(range = c(5, 25)),
  levels = 4
)

set.seed(9261979)
rf_fit <- rf_wkf |>
  tune_grid(resamples = NHANES_CV_folds, 
            grid = rf_grid,
            metrics = metric_set(rmse))

rf_fit |>
  collect_metrics() |>
  filter(.metric == "rmse") |> 
  arrange(mean)
```

#### Select the best random forest and finalize the workflow

```{r}
rf_best_params <- select_best(rf_fit, metric = "rmse")
rf_best_params

rf_final_wkf <- rf_wkf |>
  finalize_workflow(rf_best_params)

rf_final_fit <- rf_final_wkf |>
  last_fit(NHANES_split, metrics = metric_set(rmse, mae))
rf_final_model <- extract_workflow(rf_final_fit)
```

## Select the best model from each type

Again, I've chosen RMSE as the metric for these models. Now I will compare each on the test set to figure out which is working the best.

```{r}
bind_rows(
  tree_final_fit |> collect_metrics() |> mutate(Model = "Regression Tree"),
  rf_final_fit |> collect_metrics() |> mutate(Model = "Random Forest")
)
```

Okay, so the best is the regression tree model, and so I will fit that on the entire dataset.

```{r}
overall_best_model <- rf_final_wkf |>
  fit(data = NHANES)
overall_best_model
```

This is the model that I'm going to use in my API.
